title: Catalogue export
context: The content team wants a simple export of everything on the service.
task: Return the title, genre and type of every show in the catalogue.
hint: No filtering — just pick the three columns you need from the catalogue table.
answer: SELECT title, genre, type FROM shows;

title: Movies tab
context: The Movies tab should list films only, never series.
task: Return the title and runtime (duration_min) of every show that is a film rather than a series.
hint: One column tells you whether a row is a film or a series — keep only the films.
answer: SELECT title, duration_min FROM shows WHERE type = 'Movie';

title: Kids profile catalogue
context: Kids profiles may only surface the gentlest maturity ratings.
task: Return the title and maturity_rating of shows carrying any of the three kid-safe ratings: TV-Y, TV-G or PG.
hint: The rating has to be one of a short list of allowed values.
answer: SELECT title, maturity_rating FROM shows WHERE maturity_rating IN ('TV-Y','TV-G','PG');

title: Feature-length films
context: An editorial row highlights long films for a weekend binge.
task: Return the title and runtime of films that run for more than two hours.
hint: Two things must both be true: it is a film, and it is long enough. Two hours is 120 minutes.
answer: SELECT title, duration_min FROM shows WHERE type = 'Movie' AND duration_min > 120;

title: New this decade
context: A 'New this decade' row features the freshest content.
task: Return the title and release_year of shows first released in 2020 or later.
hint: Compare the release year against a cut-off, keeping that year and everything after it.
answer: SELECT title, release_year FROM shows WHERE release_year >= 2020;

title: Genre filter menu
context: The genre filter menu needs each genre listed exactly once.
task: Return every genre that appears in the catalogue, with no repeats.
hint: A genre is attached to many shows — you want each one to show up only once.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT genre FROM shows;

title: Where our subscribers are
context: Leadership wants the list of countries where we have subscribers.
task: Return each country that appears in the user base, listed only once.
hint: Many users share a country — collapse the duplicates.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users;

title: Titles beginning with 'The'
context: A quirky editorial row collects titles that open with the word 'The'.
task: Return the title of every show whose title starts with 'The ' (the word 'The' followed by a space).
hint: Pattern-match the beginning of the title text.
answer: SELECT title FROM shows WHERE title LIKE 'The %';

title: Still-running subscriptions
context: A subscription with no closing date is still active today.
task: Return the subscription_id and user_id of every subscription that has not ended.
hint: An open subscription has no end date recorded — test for the absence of a value, not an empty string.
answer: SELECT subscription_id, user_id FROM subscriptions WHERE end_date IS NULL;

title: Longest content first
context: A programming review lists the catalogue from longest runtime down.
task: Return the title and runtime of every show, longest-running first.
hint: No filter needed — just sort by runtime from high to low.
answer: SELECT title, duration_min FROM shows ORDER BY duration_min DESC;

title: Our earliest members
context: A loyalty perk rewards the very first people to sign up.
task: Return the email and signup_date of the five members who joined earliest.
hint: Order by join date with the oldest at the top, then keep only the first few.
answer: SELECT email, signup_date FROM users ORDER BY signup_date LIMIT 5;

title: Longest viewing sessions
context: The product team wants to inspect the three biggest single sittings.
task: Return the view_id, user_id and minutes_watched for the three longest individual viewing sessions.
hint: Sort the sessions by length, longest first, then take just the top few.
answer: SELECT view_id, user_id, minutes_watched FROM watch_history ORDER BY minutes_watched DESC LIMIT 3;

title: Sessions in hours
context: Product reports viewing time in hours, not minutes.
task: Return the view_id and the length of each session expressed in hours (minutes converted to hours), rounded to 2 decimals.
hint: Divide the minutes by sixty — use 60.0 so the division isn't rounded down to a whole number — and round the result.
answer: SELECT view_id, ROUND(minutes_watched / 60.0, 2) AS hours FROM watch_history;

title: Annual value of each plan
context: Finance wants to know what each subscription plan is worth over a full year.
task: Return each distinct plan alongside its yearly price (the monthly price times twelve).
hint: Compute a new column from the monthly price, and make sure each plan appears only once.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT plan, monthly_price * 12 AS yearly_price FROM subscriptions;

title: Which mail provider
context: A data-quality report groups users by their email provider.
task: Return the user_id and the domain portion of each email — everything after the '@' sign.
hint: Find the position of the '@' and take the slice of text that follows it.
answer: SELECT user_id, SUBSTR(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1) AS domain FROM users;

title: Banner text
context: Marketing renders title text in capitals on promo banners.
task: Return every show's title converted to upper case, as a column called banner.
hint: There's a function that forces text into capital letters.
answer: SELECT UPPER(title) AS banner FROM shows;

title: Series versus movies
context: The catalogue overview shows how the library splits between formats.
task: Return each type and how many titles fall under it.
hint: Collapse to one row per format, then count the titles in each.
answer: SELECT type, COUNT(*) AS title_count FROM shows GROUP BY type;

title: Big-screen viewing
context: The product team wants a single number for how much watching happens on TVs.
task: Return tv_sessions: the number of viewing sessions that took place on a TV.
hint: Count rows, but only the ones on the right device.
answer: SELECT COUNT(*) AS tv_sessions FROM watch_history WHERE device = 'TV';

title: How many people have watched?
context: Engagement reporting wants active viewers, not the number of sessions.
task: Return viewers: the number of different users who have watched at least one thing.
hint: The same user appears on many sessions — count each person once.
answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS viewers FROM watch_history;

title: Total minutes streamed
context: The headline engagement figure is total minutes watched.
task: Return total_minutes: the combined minutes watched across every session.
hint: Add up the per-session minutes into one total.
answer: SELECT SUM(minutes_watched) AS total_minutes FROM watch_history;

title: Typical sitting length
context: The dashboard shows how long an average viewing session lasts.
task: Return avg_minutes: the average length of a session, rounded to 1 decimal.
hint: Take the mean of the session minutes and round it.
answer: SELECT ROUND(AVG(minutes_watched), 1) AS avg_minutes FROM watch_history;

title: Runtime by format
context: Pricing compares the typical length of a movie against an episode.
task: Return each type and its average runtime, rounded to 1 decimal.
hint: Average the runtime separately within each format.
answer: SELECT type, ROUND(AVG(duration_min), 1) AS avg_duration FROM shows GROUP BY type;

title: How far back the library goes
context: A press fact-sheet quotes the oldest and newest release years.
task: Return oldest and newest: the earliest and latest release year in the catalogue, side by side.
hint: The smallest and the largest year, in a single row.
answer: SELECT MIN(release_year) AS oldest, MAX(release_year) AS newest FROM shows;

title: Titles per genre
context: Content strategy wants to see which genres dominate the library.
task: Return each genre and how many titles it holds.
hint: One row per genre, with a tally of titles in each.
answer: SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS title_count FROM shows GROUP BY genre;

title: Plan mix
context: Finance wants the spread of members across the plans.
task: Return each plan and how many users are on it.
hint: Collapse users to one row per plan, then count them.
answer: SELECT plan, COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM users GROUP BY plan;

title: Device mix
context: The product team ranks devices by how often they are used to watch.
task: Return each device and its session count, most-used device first.
hint: One row per device; rank by how many sessions each has.
answer: SELECT device, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM watch_history GROUP BY device ORDER BY sessions DESC, device;

title: Watch time per user
context: An engagement report totals viewing time for each member.
task: Return each user_id and their total minutes watched.
hint: Add up the minutes within each user.
answer: SELECT user_id, SUM(minutes_watched) AS total_minutes FROM watch_history GROUP BY user_id;

title: Trending titles
context: The 'Trending' row is driven by total minutes watched per show.
task: Return the show_id and total minutes watched for the five most-watched shows, highest first.
hint: Total the minutes per show, rank those totals, and keep only the leaders.
answer: SELECT show_id, SUM(minutes_watched) AS minutes FROM watch_history GROUP BY show_id ORDER BY minutes DESC, show_id LIMIT 5;

title: Our heaviest viewers
context: Retention wants members who watch unusually often.
task: Return the user_id and session count for users with more than ten viewing sessions.
hint: Count sessions per user, then keep only the groups whose tally clears the threshold.
answer: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM watch_history GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

title: Who watched what
context: Reporting needs each session labelled with the show's real title, not its id.
task: Return the user_id, the show title and minutes_watched for every viewing session.
hint: The title lives on the catalogue table — connect each session to its show through the shared id.
answer: SELECT w.user_id, s.title, w.minutes_watched FROM watch_history w JOIN shows s ON s.show_id = w.show_id;

title: Thriller engagement
context: The genre team is measuring interest in thrillers.
task: Return the view_id, show title and minutes_watched for sessions on shows in the Thriller genre.
hint: Link sessions to their show so you can see the genre, then keep only the thrillers.
answer: SELECT w.view_id, s.title, w.minutes_watched FROM watch_history w JOIN shows s ON s.show_id = w.show_id WHERE s.genre = 'Thriller';

title: Minutes captured by genre
context: Content strategy wants to know which genres soak up the most viewing time.
task: Return each genre and the total minutes watched across all its shows.
hint: Bring the genre onto each session by joining to the catalogue, then total the minutes within each genre.
answer: SELECT s.genre, SUM(w.minutes_watched) AS minutes FROM watch_history w JOIN shows s ON s.show_id = w.show_id GROUP BY s.genre;

title: Session length buckets
context: Analytics groups sessions into short, medium and long sittings.
task: Return the view_id and a bucket label: 'Long' when a session runs 60 minutes or more, 'Medium' from 25 up to 60, otherwise 'Short'.
hint: Test the ranges from the top down and hand back a label for each.
answer: SELECT view_id, CASE WHEN minutes_watched >= 60 THEN 'Long' WHEN minutes_watched >= 25 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Short' END AS bucket FROM watch_history;

title: Signups by year
context: Growth tracks how many members joined each calendar year.
task: Return the signup year as a whole number and the number of members who joined in it.
hint: Pull the year out of the signup date (as a number), then count members within each year.
answer: SELECT CAST(strftime('%Y', signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS signup_year, COUNT(*) AS signups FROM users GROUP BY signup_year;
